criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design. Discusses context of ethical issues in engineering organisations. Identifies the relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Several ethical issues (public safety, integrity, reputation) are identified and linked to engineering design; both organisational context (six-month release cycle, competition) and stakeholders are identified. However, the introduction is thin and issues are described more fully only later in the body, so not quite excellent.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions of the ethical issues. Draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Objective arguments for and against shipping are presented with reasonable depth, supported by case studies, leading to a clear conclusion. However, decision-making recommendations for different stakeholders are limited — recommendations mainly target Rachel and her company, and some arguments (competitor counterfactual) are speculative.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument, which justifies the conclusion. The body of the report follows a logical structure, with paragraphs linked and content ordered in a way that is easy to follow and support the building of the argument. Arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: The body follows a logical for/against structure building to 'The Most Ethical Path', and the conclusion follows directly from the arguments. Understanding of stakeholder impacts is sound, though some paragraphs (e.g. the competitor argument) are less developed, preventing an excellent rating.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence. Research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Arguments are substantiated with four relevant references including external case studies (NHS IT failures, VW emissions, Apple release strategy) and the EA Code of Ethics. Evidence is mostly qualitative; little quantitative data (e.g. fine figures, defect rates) is cited, so not excellent.

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections which serve their respective functions well: abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion. Maps, figures, tables, and any visual elements are correctly used to support written discussions. The writing is free from any grammatical errors. The expression is fluent, has appropriate word choice, is concise, easy to read and understand. References are well-structured and appropriate providing strong support of the motivations in the report.

overall: A competent, well-structured ethics report with clear for/against arguments, relevant case studies (NHS, VW) and a justified recommendation. Weakened by an underdeveloped introduction, no visual elements, several language/typographical errors, the 'EACE' misuse, and limited stakeholder-specific decision guidance. Estimated 38/50.

feedback.summary: You produced a competent, well-structured ethics report with clear for/against arguments, relevant case studies (NHS HSSIB, Volkswagen, Apple) and a justified recommendation not to ship. Your introduction identifies stakeholders and ethical issues, and your conclusion follows from your reasoning. To reach the top band, deepen stakeholder-specific decision guidance, add quantitative evidence, include visual elements, and proofread carefully.
next_steps: In 'The Most Ethical Path', add explicit decision-making guidance for each stakeholder (chip contractor, health department, end-users), not just Rachel and her company.
Strengthen arguments with quantitative evidence, e.g. defect rates, recall costs or fine figures from your case studies, and replace the speculative competitor counterfactual with sourced support.
Add at least one figure or table (e.g. a stakeholder-impact matrix or decision trade-off table), and proofread headings and grammar throughout.

criteria.C1: Very good (8/10). Your introduction identifies several ethical issues — public safety, integrity, reputation — and links them to engineering design, naming stakeholders such as Rachel, her company, the chip contractor and the health department. To reach Excellent, develop the introduction itself more fully so the issues and their significance are described there, rather than emerging later in the body.
criteria.C2: Very good (8/10). You present objective arguments for and against shipping with reasonable depth, supported by case studies, and reach a clear conclusion. For Excellent, extend decision-making recommendations to several different stakeholders and avoid speculative arguments, such as the unevidenced competitor counterfactual ('what's to say one of her competitors won't take the deal').
criteria.C3: Very good (8/10). Your body follows a logical for/against structure building to 'The Most Ethical Path', and your conclusion follows directly from your arguments, showing sound understanding of stakeholder impacts. For Excellent, make every paragraph compelling — the competitor argument in particular needs fuller development so the whole argument systematically covers all stakeholders.
criteria.C4: Very good (8/10). Your arguments are substantiated with four relevant references, including the NHS HSSIB, Volkswagen and Apple cases and the EA Code of Ethics [2]. Evidence is mostly qualitative; for Excellent, add quantitative data (e.g. emissions-fine figures, defect or failure rates) and check that reference [1] genuinely supports your competitive-advantage claim.
criteria.C5: Good (6/10). Your report has the correct structure (abstract, introduction, body, conclusion) and IEEE-style references, but contains no figures, tables or visual elements, which caps this criterion. Several language errors also appear: 'DICUSSION', 'ofprofessional', 'series ofIT', 'benefits of could', 'have her company might go under', and repeated use of 'EACE' instead of EA. Reference [3] needs a URL and complete accessed dates.
